newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hundreds surround court as Vietnam trial nears end.
newsitem.headline: Hundreds surround court as Vietnam trial nears end.

text.p: Hundreds of people surrounded a court in central Hanoi on Wednesday during scenes of near chaos as judges began reading out the verdicts in Vietnam's biggest-yet drugs trial.

Police wielding electric batons or riding through the throngs on motorbikes with sidecars attempted to keep the crowds back, as people crammed the area outside the building or climbed on to rooftops to watch the scene below.

Inside the court, judges were reading out a 100-page summing up and verdict, which would send state security officials, border guards and other members of a trafficking ring either to jail or the firing squad.

Earlier in the day newspapers had been packed with last-minute details of the two-week trial, whose central figures have become household names, and even the father of key defendant Vu Xuan Truong said his son deserved to die.
The trial of the 22 people, half of them former police and border security officials, is the biggest drugs scandal yet to surface in communist Vietnam.
The judges were expected to follow a prosecution recommendation calling for eight people, including two women, to be sentenced to death.
However, sources at the court said leniency might be shown towards the women, who maintained their innocence throughout the proceedings.
Eight of the 14 others are expected to face life imprisonment, with the rest set for terms of up to 20 years.
Truong, a former captain in the Interior Ministry's anti-crime unit has already accepted that he will die.

He has tried to commit suicide twice, first by dashing his head against the wall of his prison-cell wall and then by butting the corner of a water cistern, and has taken to wearing a white headband to mourn his own coming death.
Truong's father, Vu Van Vuong, told the Lao Dong newspaper that his son deserved to die. But he called for law to deal humanely with Truong's co-defendant wife and brother.
The drugs syndicate is believed to have flooded the country with an estimated 300 kg (660 lb) of heroin from the remote corners of Thailand, Laos and Burma over several years.
